text:
Verses 100-108

This section of verses refers back to stories of the prophets recounted above, providing a holistic overview of them that expounds God’s habit of dealing with His servants and the destruction in this world and eternal punishment in the Hereafter that are the consequences of idolatry for wrongdoing nations, as a lesson for the attentive.

(11:100) These are from the accounts of (min) the townships which We recount to you. Of them there are some that still stand, and some that have been mown down.

The demonstrative pronoun, ‘These’ refers to the stories recounted above. The use of the preposition min conveys the meaning of portioning (tabʿīḍ). In other words: ‘What we recounted to you here is just a portion of accounts about the townships, regions, and their inhabitants.’

Of them there are some that still stand, and some that have been mown down—Here, God invokes the metaphor of agricultural crops, where some are still standing and others have been harvested.

If this refers to the cities themselves, it suggests that some of the cities whose stories We have related to you are still standing, their remnants not destroyed. For example, the cities of Lot’s people, at the time their story was revealed in the Qur’an, as stated: Certainly W e have left of it a manifest sign for a people who apply reason (29:35), and: And indeed you pass by

them at dawn and at night. So do you not apply reason? (37:138). Then there some others that have been completely erased, their landmarks obliterated, such that not even ruins remain—like the cities of Noah’s people and ʿĀd. On the other hand, if it refers to the inhabitants of these cities, it means that some of these nations and peoples are still standing, their ruin not yet complete, like Noah’s and Ṣāliḥ’s nations. And some have had their end decreed by God, like Lot’s people, from whom only Lot’s family was spared, and Lot was not originally one of them.

(11:101) We did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves.

Of no avail to them were their gods whom they would invoke besides Allah, in any wise, when your Lord’s edict came, and they did not increase them in anything but ruin.

This means that God did not wrong them by inflicting divine punishment on them and bringing about their destruction following their idolatry

and transgression. Rather, they wronged themselves when they committed idolatry and forsook any obedience to God. If there is an action and there is a punishment prescribed for it, one of the two must be unjust, either the act itself or the punishment it warrants. If the punishment is not unjust, then the action that brings the punishment must be unjust.

In short, the meaning is: ‘We punished them for their wrongdoings.’ Therefore, the statement, Of no avail to them were their gods whom they would invoke besides Allah …, based on the arrangement of the verse, means: ‘We seized them with punishment and their gods, whom they invoked besides God to bring them good and protect them from harm, did not avail them in the least when God’s edict came to pass and they were sentenced to His punishment … or when their Lord’s punishment upon them

became due.’

… and they did not increase them in anything but ruin (tatbīb)— Tatbīb, derived from tabb,means to devastate something (tadmīr) or annihilate it (ihlāk). Its original meaning is to ‘to cut.’ This is because their worship of idols was a sin for which they were deserving of punishment. And when they tasted God’s punishment and violence, they turned to their idols and pleaded with them for relief. However, this supplication to their idols was also a sin, so it only served to intensify their punishment and make the penalty harsher for them. Hence, it did not increase them in anything except ruin.

Attributing their ruin to their gods is an example of metaphorical language, as, in reality, it refers to their supplication to these gods, which is the action of the one who is supplicating, not the one who is being supplicated to.

(11:102) Such is the seizing of your Lord when He seizes the townships that are wrongdoing. Indeed His seizing is painful, severe.

The demonstrative pronoun ‘such’ serves as a reference to past events, specifically to the accounts of the towns presented above, which are some instances of God’s retribution. In this verse, the unlimited divine punishment is being compared with the punishment inflicted upon them, stating: ‘His retribution is universally painful and severe.’ This statement is

an example of a simile that compares a general idea to particular instances of it, indicating that the predication it reflects is not solely applicable to the instances mentioned but rather is general, encompassing all individuals. This is a common type of simile. The statement, Indeed His seizing is

painful, severe, serves to explain the basis of the simile, which is the pain and severity of His punishment.

Therefore, the meaning of this passage is as follows: ‘Just as God Almighty punished earlier wrongdoing nations—such as the peoples of Noah, Hūd, Ṣāliḥ, Lot, Shuʿayb, and Pharaoh—with a severe and painful punishment, so too will He punish the rest of the wrongdoing towns

when He seizes them. Those who reflect should draw a lesson from this.’

(11:103) There is indeed a sign in that for him who fears the punishment of the Hereafter. That is a day on which all mankind

will be gathered, and it is a day witnessed.

The demonstrative pronoun ‘that’ refers to what God has informed us about the stories of those wrongdoing towns that He seized with a severe and painful punishment on account of their misdeeds. Here, He informs us that His punishment of the other wrongdoers will be likewise painful and severe, and says that this is a sign for those who fear the punishment of the Hereafter and an indication that God Almighty will seize the criminals for their crimes after they die. His punishment will surely be severe and painful, which means that people should draw a lesson from this and take precautions against bringing down God’s wrath upon themselves.

That is a day for which all mankind will be gathered (yawmun majmūʿun la-hu al-nās) means that the day on which the punishment of the afterlife occurs is a day when people will be gathered. Therefore, the demonstrative pronoun ‘that’ is a reference to the day indicated by the mention of the punishment of the afterlife. According to some commentators,

it is for this reason that it is used in the masculine form (dhālik instead of the feminine tilka), but it could also be that the demonstrative is used in the masculine to match its predicate (‘day’, which is also masculine). The description of the Last Day as a day ‘for which all mankind will be gathered’ (which is an adjectival construct) rather than saying ‘people will gather for it’ (sa-yajmaʿu la-hu al-nās), is to indicate that the gathering of people is one of the day’s definitive characteristics, which it possesses inherently without needing to be associated with it through a predicate. The distinctive characteristic of this day is that people are gathered for it, and the lām in la-hu,indicates purpose. Therefore, this day has a purpose that can only be achieved by gathering humankind in a way that leaves no one absent. Equally, people have a role which connects each one of them to the totality. In doing so, the first intermingles with the last and the last with the first, and all are mixed with some and some with all. This role is the reckoning of their deeds in terms of faith and disbelief, obedience and disobedience, and generally in terms of happiness and misery.

It is clear that a single action of a single human being is derived from all his previous actions related to his internal states, and all his subsequent actions also depend on his heart’s condition. Similarly, one’s action is related to the actions of the rest of his species in terms of infiuencing others and being influenced by them. Similarly, the deeds of the first generations are related to the deeds of the later ones, and the deeds of the later

generations are related to the deeds of the previous ones. Among the earlier generations are the leaders of guidance and misguidance, who are responsible for the deeds of the later ones, and among the later ones are the followers and dependents, responsible for the delusions and conceitedness

of their predecessors. God Almighty says, W e will surely question those to whom the messengers were sent, and W e will surely question the messengers.

(7:6), and He said, “ Indeed it is We who revive the dead and write what they have sent ahead and what they left behind, and We have figured everything in a m anifest register (36:12).

Divine retribution, then, inevitably follows from God’s decisive judgement.

And this matter, as described here, only comes about when a group of people gathers in such a way that none are excluded.

From this, it appears that the issue of individual human beings in their graves and their recompense therein with some form of reward or punishment—as indicated by the verses of the Qur’an on the isthmus (barzakh) and detailed in the reports from the Prophet and the Imams of the Household of the Prophet —is distinct from what God Almighty has told us about the account on the Day of Resurrection and the recompense decreed therein in the form of eternal Heaven or Hell. W hat awaits a person in the isthmus is the completion of the record of their deeds, to be kept in store for the Day of Judgement. And what they experience there in the isthmus, whether in the form of a paradise or a fire, is but a precursor to the final judgement and recompense that awaits them thereafter. W hat is there is not a complete accounting, nor a final judgement, nor a full recompense. This is hinted at in verses such as the Fire, to which they are exposed

morning and evening. And on the day when the Hour sets in Pharaoh’s clan will enter the severest punishment (40:46), and they are dragged into scalding waters and then set aflame in the Fire (40:71–72). The first verse describes their punishment as being exposed to the fire, and then on the Day of Resurrection, entering it fully, which is described as ‘the severest punishment’; while the second verse speaks about their being punished by being dragged through boiling water and then being set aflame in the Fire. Consider the verse about those slain in the way of God: rather they are living and provided for near their Lord, exulting in what Allah has given them out of His grace, and rejoicing for those who have not yet joined them from behind them that they will have no fear, nor will they grieve (3:170). This verse is explicitly about the world of the grave that comes before the Day of Judgement, as it does not mention a reckoning or an eternal paradise, but it mentions some enjoyments generally.

Now consider the verse: W hen death comes to one of them, he says, ‘M y Lord! Take me back, that I may act righteously in what I have left behind.’ ‘By no means! These are mere words that he says.’ And ahead of them is a barrier until the day they will be resurrected (23:99–100). This verse says that,

after death, people find themselves in an interstitial life that exists between the worldly life, which is play and amusement, and the afterlife, which is the real life. As He says: The life of this world is nothing but diversion and play, but the abode of the Hereafter is indeed Life, had they known! (29:64). In summary, the earthly life is the realm of action, the intermediate realm (known as barzakh or the isthmus) is the domain of preparation for the final judgement and recompense, and the afterlife is the domain of judgement and recompense. As God has said: on the day when Allah will not let the Prophet down and the faithful who are with him. Their light will move swiftly before them and on their right. They will say, ‘Our Lord! Perfect our light for us, and forgive us! (66:8). They arrive there, with the light they earned in the earthly life, which they prepared in the intermediate realm, and then, on the Day of Resurrection, they ask for the completion of their light and the removal of whatever remains upon them of the

world of diversion and play.

The phrase, and it is a day witnessed (11:103), appears to follow on from the previous sentence, That is a day for which all mankind will be gathered, because the gathering of people on that day necessitates the presence of witnesses. However, this phrase does not only refer to humankind. The fact that it is used without any qualification suggests that this is a day witnessed by all of those who have the capacity to witness: humans, angels, and jinn alike. There are many verses indicating the presence of the jinn and devils and the presence of the angels on the Day of Judgement, and these support the most general meaning of witnessing that we have mentioned here.

(11:104) And We do not defer it but for a determinate term.

This means that there is a set time for that day, which God has ordained not to occur before its due time. Now, God judges, and none can repeal His judgement or resist His decree, therefore it must come to pass. Note that, according to the verse, God only delays the Day of Judgement for a preordained period, so when the time is complete and the term arrives, His decree is realized, and the day sets in.

(11:105) The day it comes, no one shall speak except by His leave.

Some of them will be wretched and some felicitous.

The pronoun ‘it’ in ‘the day it comes’ refers back to the ‘determinate term’ mentioned in the previous verse. In other words, on the day when the determinate term, to which the resurrection has been deferred, comes, no soul will speak except by His permission. As God has said: Whoever expects to encounter Allah, Allah’s time will indeed come (29:5).

Some, like al-Ṭabrisī in Majmaʿ al-bayān, have understood ‘the day it comes’ as a referring to ‘the daythe Resurrection and divine recompensecomes’, based on the fact that the previous verse also refers to these.

However, this is a rather tortuous reading of the verse, and one which is not necessary given the explanation we have presented.

Others, such Rashīd Riḍā writing in al-M anār, have read the verse as meaning, ‘at the time that particular day arrives, no rational soul will speak except by God’s permission.’ Therefore, the intended meaning of ‘day’ in the verse is a time in the general sense of the word, rather than a specific duration thereof, because this is the time when a the specific day described in the verse will come to pass, and this specific day is what the pronoun ‘it’ refers to in ‘the day it comes.’

However, this reading is incorrect because it necessitates that ‘the day’ (in the sense of ‘the time’) be an adverb for ‘the day’ (the specific day, or the Day of Judgement), which essentially reduces the meaning of the verse to ‘at the time when that particular time comes’ or ‘the day when that particular day comes.’ Now, while one could differentiate between the two days

to make one of them specific and the other general (as Rashīd Riḍā does in his commentary), this does not help to avoid the problematic implication of something being an adverb for itself, and time (which is an adverb

in itself) being the adverb for another time. After all, this is impossibility that cannot be resolved by merely changing the wording.

Distinguishing between ‘day’ in the general sense and ‘day’ in the specific one results in a purely conceptual distinction that does not provide

any substantive value for our understanding of the verse. This is because, when we say ‘the day when the specified day arrives’, the first and second days both refer to the same thing, as they are co-extensive with one another. However, it can happen that a specific time is associated with an event that occurs during that time, such that the time itself can be spoken of as one event among others. This negates its adverbial aspect, and then such a time is considered the adverbial for another time. For instance, one might say: ‘The Day of Sacrifice during the month of Dhū al-Hijja’ and ‘The Day of Ashura in the month of Muharram.’ As God says, and when the Hour sets in (22:55). So, if this specific concern is valid in the verse, it is possible

that the pronoun ‘it’ in ‘the day it comes’ refers to the day itself. … no one shall speak except by His leave (lā takallamu nafsun illā bi idhni-hi)—This means that no soul amongst those assembled will speak except by the permission of God. Note that the verb takallamu was originally tatakallamu, but the first ta- was omitted, as is a common convention

in the Arabic language.

The preposition bi in illābi idhni-hi (‘except by His leave’) signifies accompaniment. Therefore, in reality, the exception applies to the speech rather than the speaker. This is evident in His saying, None shall speak except whom the All-beneficent permits (78:38). The implication here is that no soul will utter anything unless its speech is accompanied by His permission, unlike worldly speech in which one can say whatever they please, whether or not God has granted them moral permission to do so. The attribute, namely no soul will speak except by His permission, is mentioned as one of the special characteristics that define the Day of Resurrection. Yet, it is not exclusive to it. Indeed, no soul ever speaks, nor any incident occurs, except by His permission, without this being specific to the Day of Resurrection.

It has been mentioned in some of our previous discussions that the majority of the distinctive qualities of the Day of Resurrection presented in the Qur’an are not, in fact, limited to it alone. This includes the verses: The day when they will emerge, nothing about them will be hidden from Allah

(40:16); … a day when you will turn back, not having anyone to protect you from Allah (40:33); It is a day when no soul will be of any avail to another soul and all command that day will belong to Allah (82:19).

There are other verses besides these also.

However, none of these qualities are unique to the Day of Resurrection. After all, it is obvious that nothing is ever hidden from God, nor can anything ever offer protection from Him, and neither does any soul have

power over any other except by His leave, and He has eternal authority over creation and command.

However, something else becomes apparent when we contemplate on other verses.

For example, God quotes His own speech on the Day of Resurrection:

‘You were certainly oblivious of this. W e have removed your veil from you, and so your sight is acute today’ (50:22); And the speech of the guilty ones: ‘Our Lord! We have seen and heard. Send us back so that we may act righteously. Indeed we are now convinced.’ (32:12); On the day when We gather them all together, W e shall say to those who ascribe partners, ‘Stay where you are— you and your partners!’ Then We shall set them apart from one another… There every soul will examine what it has sent in advance, and they will be returned to Allah, their real master, and what they used to fabricate will forsake them (10:28–30).

Reflecting on these verses, we note that the Day of Resurrection is an event in which God will assemble His servants and remove the curtains and veils that are in front of them, thereby revealing truths fully, and unveiling what is behind the cover of the Unseen in this creation. At this point,

there will be no longer any doubt or hesitation in their breasts, nor will any whisper of disbelief stir in their hearts. They will witness utterly that God is the Manifest Truth, they will see that all power belongs to God, and that dominion, protection, command, and control belong to Him alone with no partner having any share in them.

The system of causes and effects, which they once perceived as existing independently of God, now cease to exist, severing the links and dissolving the causal relations between different things. At this point, the stars of causation scatter and the constellations that previously guided their suppositions in their darkness vanish. No sovereign retains any independent rule,

no person of authority or power has anything to reinforce their status, no object has a refuge or sanctuary to which it can turn or with which it can take shelter in order to seek its protection. There is no veil that can hide one thing from another or obscure it. Every matter is under the control of the One, All-dominant God, and no one else possesses sovereignty.

This is the meaning of His saying: The day when they will emerge, nothing about them will be hidden from Allah; His saying: … not having anyone to protect you from Allah; and His saying: It is a day when no soul will be of any avail to another soul and all command that day will belong to Allah. This is reflected in many other verses of the Qur’an, all of which all deny the illusions with which people’s minds adorn this worldly existence, which is nothing more than diversion and play. Indeed, in their conjectures, these causes assume the meaning of causation, and are garbed with the attributes of sovereignty, authority, power, protection, honor, and dignity in a genuinely independent manner. They are considered the givers, the preventers, the beneficial, and the harmful, with no goal beyond them and no goodness apart from them.

Based on this, we can infer the real meaning of His saying: The day it comes, no one shall speak except by His leave. This meaning is reiterated in other verses with similar phrasing such as His saying: None shall speak except whom the All-beneficent permits and who says what is right (78:38), and His saying: This is a day wherein they will not speak (77:35).

This is because God describes this Day in the following terms: on the day when the secrets are examined (86:9), and: whether you disclose what is in your hearts or hide it, Allah will bring you to account for it (2:284). Thus, it is evident that the reckoning on the Day of Resurrection is based on what is in peoples souls, of good and evil states and attributes, not what is revealed by means of discovery as is the case in this worldly existence. Therefore, whatever is hidden beneath the veils of secrecy in this world, including the inner depths of human souls and the hidden aspects of peoples’ hearts, will be revealed and stripped of any covering on the Day of Resurrection. What is unknown today will be evident tomorrow. The language we, as a society, use in our interactions, is nothing more than a series of sounds joined to one another. They point, as a matter of convention and thought, to meanings that reside in our consciousness. We adopt

and exchange these sounds primarily due to our societal need to understand what is in the minds of others, due to our inability to perceive this directly through our senses.

Our use of language is a societal mechanism to which we resort in order to reveal the ideas hidden in our respective consciousness. This mechanism allows us to express what lies within our minds that would otherwise be beyond human comprehension. Had we been endowed with a sense that enabled us to directly perceive intellectual meanings in the same way as our sight enables us to perceive light and colors, or the way our touch enables us to sense heat and cold, roughness and smoothness, then we would not need to fashion languages and communicate through them. There would be no words or speech among us. Similarly, if human life was solitary rather than social, there would be no concept of speech or even a seed of its existence. This is because worldly life is composed of both what is perceivable and what is beyond perception—the visible and the Unseen. People are in dire need of revealing what is in their minds, their intentions, and having these understood by others. If we imagine a purely observable existence, where life consisted only of matters that could be perceived, there would be no need for speech and language whatsoever. If we were to apply the term ‘speech’ to any existing state in such a life, it would merely refer to some of what is in people’s minds being made apparent to others, and those others becoming aware of it.

This kind of existence, characterized as such, is the existence of Resurrection Day, as God describes it in phrases such as the day when the secrets are examined (86:9). This is further evidenced by God’s words: On that day neither humans will be questioned about their sins nor jinn … The guilty will be recognized by their mark; so they will be seized by the forelocks and the feet (55:41). If you argue that, in such a scenario, there would be no sense in lies and deceit taking place there, the Qur’an affirms precisely the opposite in the following verse: On the day when We gather them all together, W e shall say to those who ascribed partners (to Allah) ‘W here are your partners that you used to claim?’ Then their only excuse will be to say, ‘By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists.’ Look, how they forswear themselves, and what they used to fabricate has forsaken them! (6:22–24); as well

as in the verse: The day when Allah will raise them all together, they will swear to Him, just like they swear to you (now), supposing that they stand on something. Look! They are indeed liars! (58:18).

Author’s comment: This refers to the manifestation of inner characteristics, just as a person, when thinking, perceives the depths of his own mind without needing to inform himself about his thoughts or reveal his innermost feelings to himself verbally. This is because he bears witness to his own inner self, not to something unknown or foreign to him. Nonetheless, he conjures an image of speech that signifies the meanings he perceives in his mind. Perhaps he even verbalizes these thoughts, articulating the components of the idea that crosses his mind with language. His

motivation for doing so is his habit of speaking and pronouncing the thoughts that exist in his mind to others.

The polytheists and hypocrites portrayed in these verses, having grown accustomed to deceit and falsehood in their worldly life and having lived this life on the basis of such delusions, reveal their true nature on the day when inherent characteristics and traits of the soul became apparent. Otherwise, it is impossible to imagine a person standing before his Lord— God the Most High—who scrutinizes his inner and outer self, with his deeds clearly presented, his record laid bare, in the presence of witnesses, his body parts testifying to what they did while he was alive, and all the means to which a person might take recourse besides God—including lies— vanishing into nothingness, and his secrets made public, and yet he continues to lie in the hope of deceiving God, presenting a false, deceptive argument and hoping to escape through this.

This is like when, on the Day of Resurrection, they are commanded to prostrate themselves, but they are unable to do so. God says: The day when the catastrophe occurs, and they are summoned to prostrate themselves, they will not be able to do so. W ith a humbled look (in their eyes), they will be overcast by abasement. Certainly, they were summoned to prostrate themselves while they were yet sound (68:43). Their inability to prostrate is due to

the fact that arrogance has become entrenched in their souls. Had it been due to God preventing them from doing so on that day, this would have been an argument in their favor against Him rather than an argument in His favor against them.

Poser: If it is as you say it is, and there is neither any need for speech nor any occurrence thereof, then what is the meaning of the exception in the verse, no one shall speak except by His leave, and other similar statements we find in the Qur’an? And why does God recount what they will say on the Day of Judgement in various parts of His Book?

Reply: There is no doubt that a person, in his existence, has a choice in his actions, including speech. He has an equal propensity to perform an action and to abstain from it, which are equivalent relative to him. W hen he commits an act, one of the options has inevitably been chosen. There is no choice after that. The inevitable consequences that follow from the action, including the recompense that the person has earned through the action, are just like the action itself after it has been realized in external reality— all follow inevitably from it.

Now, the Hereafter is a realm of recompense, not a realm of deeds.

There, human free will does not exist; what remains is the individual and the actions they have performed, which are now inseparably attached to them as a matter of necessity. Along with these actions are the written records of their deeds, the witnesses to these deeds, and their Lord, to whom all matters return, and by whose decree all judgements are made. When summoned, they respond out of compulsion, as God says, On that day they will follow a summoner in whom there will be no deviousness

(20:108). In the worldly life, they were called to the truth, but they did not respond.

If they are asked to speak in the Hereafter, their speech does not resemble the worldly speech which originated from their own free will and

revealed what was hidden in their souls. Their mouths are sealed; there is no way for them to express what they wish. And how could they, when God has said, Today We shall seal their mouths, and their hands shall speak to Us, and their feet shall bear witness concerning what they used to earn (36:65), and “This is a day wherein they will not speak, nor will they be permitted to offer excuses. (77:35–36).

Excuses only make sense when it comes to recompense that involves an element of choice, for such recompense could either exist or not exist. However, the bad deeds that one has unquestionably committed, and the inevitable punishment that follows, cannot be a subject of excuses, because there is no choice involved. As God says, “‘O faithless ones! Do not make any excuses today. You are only being requited for what you used to do’ (66:7). In other words, your recompense is identical with the actions you have performed; no excuse or argument can change that. It would only be different if the recompense were taking place in this world and in the hands

of a judge who can decide what they see as most appropriate.

In sum, if one speaks out of being asked on the Day of Resurrection, their speech is out of compulsion and aligns with their deeds, which have been made manifest and, therefore, cannot be hidden at all in that realm. If they lie in their speech, this would be nothing more than an expression of their innermost nature, as we have previously mentioned, and it would be considered one of their deeds that will be revealed—not a genuine response to a question. Their mouths will be sealed, and their hearing, sight, skin, hands, and legs will be made to speak. The deeds they have performed will be brought forward, the witnesses will testify, and God is a witness over everything.

To summarize all the preceding points, the meaning of God’s statement, no one shall speak except by His leave, is that people’s speech on that

day will not be like their speech in this world. It will not be a voluntary disclosure of their inner thoughts that permits the speaker to either lie or tell the truth. This volitional control, which is an integral part of the realm of deeds (this world), is abolished in the Hereafter. A person has no free will in their speech because it is tied to God’s permission and His will. If you contemplate deeply, you will find that the outcome of this feature— the removal of human free will concerning speech and all other actions, and the encompassing nature of compulsion—leads back to what we initially discussed: the characteristic feature of the Day of Resurrection is the unveiling of the realities of all things and the transformation of the Unseen into the seen.

We advise the reader to pay close attention to the insights offered by the divine discourse about the Hereafter, for it is a complex and profound puzzle.

Some scholars have suggested that the meaning of the phrase, “ no one shall speak except by His leave, is that speech is only allowed if it is decent and permitted under religious law. People would naturally refrain from indecent speech in that realm, hence only decent and permissible speech occurs.

However, this is an arbitrary restriction of the verse’s meaning. After all, as we have already discussed, the Day of Judgement is not a day of action to permit good deeds or forbid bad ones. The refuge here, born out of the circumstances of recompense rather than action, does not distinguish between good and bad actions, even though both are choices, because the moral categories of good or bad can only apply to actions in which the person doing them has free will.

However, God Almighty says, no one shall speak except by His leave, and it is well known that presenting excuses is not in of itself a morally blameworthy act.

Other commentators have said that the meaning of the verse is that no one will speak beneficial words in the hereafter, such as words of intercession or mediation, except by His permission.

This reading of the verse understands it along similar lines to verses such as, Intercession will not avail that day except from him whom the Allbeneficent allows and approves of his word (20:109). However, this also

narrows the meaning of the verse without any evidence to support such a restriction. If this was indeed the intended meaning, it would have been more appropriate to say: ‘no soul speaks on behalf of another soul or about it, except by His permission,’ similar to His saying, no soul will be of any avail to another soul (82:19).

W hat we have presented above provides a way to reconcile verses that appear to affirm that people will speak on the Day of Resurrection with those that appear to deny the same thing.

This is as follows: The verses that concern the matter of speaking on the Day of Resurrection fall into two categories:

The first category denies speech or affirms it for all people without exception, as in His saying, On that day neither humans will be questioned about their sins nor jinn (55:39), and His saying, The day when every soul will com e pleading for itself (16:111).

The second category denies any form of speech, whether truthful or false, as we see in the verse, This is a day wherein they will not speak (77:35), and His saying, quoting the wrongdoers: ‘Now we have no intercessors, nor do we have any sympathetic friend’ (26:101).

Verses of the first category can be reconciled through reference to verses such as, None shall speak except whom the All-beneficent permits and who says what is right (78:38). While the apparent conflict between verses of the second category can be resolved by the verse presently under discussion, no one shall speak except by His leave (11:105). However, based on the

explanation given above, this suggests that they are bound in their speech to say only what God permits: they cannot freely choose and express what they wish as they could in this world. This is one of the unique attributes of the Day of Resurrection.

Based on this, the shortcomings of the explanation offered by Rashīd Riḍā in al-Manār become evident. For example, he says of the present verse: ‘The denial that any speech will occur on that day, except by His permission, explains the reconciliation between verses categorically negating it and those affirming it. He had mentioned verses such as, This is a day

wherein they will not speak (77:35), and, Today We shall seal their mouths

(36:65).

However, the problems with his explanation are, first of all, that he failed to distinguish between the two different categories of verses on this topic. This suggests that the denial that any speech will take place except by God’s permission, as mentioned in the present verse, sufiices to resolve the apparent conflict between the different verses, which is not the case. Secondly, he did not explain what it meant for someone to speak by God’s permission, which means that the verse is presenting something as a unique feature of the Day of Resurrection, when this does not appear to be something exclusive to it.

One way to address this apparent contradiction is to say that the Day of Resurrection consists of situations where people are permitted to speak in some of them but not in others. And this reading is supported by some narrations.

However, while this answer might appear to differ from the previous one at first glance, it does not, in reality, eliminate the question of what is meant by God’s permission, and essentially returns to it.

Another answer might be that what is meant by the absence of speech is that people will not speak with arguments sound, rather they will speak by confessing their sins. Some may also blame others, and some may ascribe sins to others. According to this reading, the phrase, no one shall speak except by His leave is a akin to telling someone who has spoken at length without presenting any convincing argument, ‘You have not said anything.’ Those who speak without presenting a sound argument are considered not to be speaking, because they do not meet the requirement of speech, which should include an argument. It is as though their speech isn’t considered genuine speech. So the negation of speech refers to the dismissal of speech that serves no purpose besides making empty claims.

However, if this explanation was correct, it would only apply to verses such as, This is a day wherein they will not speak (77:35). However, in the case of verses like, None shall speak except whom the All-beneficent permits

(78:38), it still does not solve the problem.

Another possible answer is the one presented by al-Alūsī1, which he quotes from al-Ghurar wa al-Durar of Sharīfial-Murtaḍā, that the Day of Resurrection is an exceptionally long day. Hence, it is possible that speaking would be forbidden in certain times and places but permitted at others. However, the problem with this explanation is that in referring to the Day of Judgement in terms of its length, it renders the meaning of the verse, This is a day wherein they will not speak (77:35) as ‘This is a day wherein for a part of it they will not speak.’ However, this reading of the verse contradicts its apparent meaning. The same problem arises with the second

explanation, which focuses on the differing stages of the Day of Judgement. In fact, both of these explanations—that is the second and the fourth of those presented here— ultimately lead back to the same problem. The difference between the two is that the second one resolves the contradiction

by distinguishing between different locations on the Day of Judgement, while the fourth one resolves it by distinguishing between different times therein, just as the third one resolves it by distinguishing between different kinds of speech—some beneficial and some not.

A fifth possible response can be derived from the claim some scholars make that the exception in the verse, no one shall speak except by His leave

(11:105) is discontinuous. In other words, it means that no soul can speak of its own ability, except by God’s permission. Essentially, this reading posits that the forbidden speech on the Day of Judgement is the speech that originates from human capacity, while the permissible speech is that which occurs by God’s permission.

However, the problem with this is that human speech, like all other voluntary actions, does not solely depend on the capability of the human being. Instead, it is attributed to human capacity, which is itself derived from God’s power and permission. So, whenever a human speaks or performs an action using their own capacity, this is produced through their

capability that is accompanied by God’s permission. The meaning of the exception in this context is the elimination of all the factors contributing to speech on the Day of Judgement except for one, that is, God’s permission. Consequently, the exception is connected and goes back to what we initially proposed: The prohibited speech is voluntary, similar to worldly speech, while the permissible speech is that which is solely based on divine causation, which is with His permission and will. In the scenario the situation is one of compulsion and taking recourse to God. However, proponents of this explanation believe that the reason for this compulsion on

the Day of Judgement is witnessing its horrors, as people, when faced with these horrors, are compelled to confess, admit, speak honestly, and follow the truth. We have already discussed that the reason for this is the situation being one of recompense rather than free-willed actions, and the fact that it is merely the unveiling of realities rather than the choice of human beings. The passage, Some of them will be wretched and some felicitous, presents felicity (saʿāda) and wretchedness (shiqāwa) as two opposing states.

The felicity of any being is to attain the goodness which completes its existence and brings it delight. For human beings, who are composed of both a body and a soul, this means attaining goodness according to both their physical and spiritual powers, experiencing pleasure and satisfaction from it. Conversely, their misery arises from the loss or deprivation of this goodness. These two states, as per common parlance, relate to the existence or non-existence of a trait (malaka), and the difference between felicity and goodness is that happiness is a specific good for a species or individual, while goodness is more general in nature.

The apparent meaning of the verse, Some of them will be wretched and some felicitous, does not indicate that all beings must fall exclusively into these two categories. However, it does fit with God’s division of people into believers, disbelievers, and those who have diminished capacity, such as children and the mentally ill, or those who have not received clear guidance in this life. However, the main aim of these verses is not to categorise

people according to their deeds and deserved outcomes, but to emphasize the nature of the Day of Judgement. It is a day when all people will be gathered and none will be absent, and it ends in either Paradise or Hellfire. Those who are of diminished capacity may represent a third category, distinct from those who earn Paradise through their deeds and those who deserve Hellfire through theirs. However, it is necessary that these individuals do not simply vanish or remain in an intermediate state of waiting

forever. In the hereafter, they will ultimately join one of the two groups: the felicitous or the wretched, entering either Paradise or Hellfire. As stated in Sūrah al-Tawba: others waiting Allah’s edict: either He shall punish them, or turn to them clemently, and Allah is all-knowing, all-wise (9:106). Therefore, the gathering of humankind on the Day of Judgement ultimately includes only these two groups: the felicitous and the wretched,

with everyone being either one or the other.

This passage is similar to another verse in the Qur’an, and warn of the Day of Gathering, in which there is no doubt, a part will be in paradise and a part will be in the Blaze (42:8). Here, the statement, a part will be in paradise and a part will be in the Blaze implies exclusivity, especially in the given context, even though it doesn’t necessarily imply so on its own. The verse suggests that among the people gathered on that Day, some will be wretched, characterized by misery, while others will be felicitous, imbued with happiness. As for when these descriptors become firmly attached to the individuals and whether these attributes are inherent or determined by an irrevocable divine decree, or if they are established through personal actions and deeds, with the individuals originally free from either set of characteristics, the verse does not specify. However, the placement of the verse in the context of calling for faith and righteous deeds and urging people to choose obedience and avoid sin, indicates that the path to happiness or misery can be facilitated by one’s deeds, as stated in

Sūrah ʿAbasa (80:20), Then He made the way easy for him.

From this, it becomes clear that there is a fiaw in the explanation some scholars have offered for this verse. They believe that it shows that an individual’s state of felicity or wretchedness is predetermined by God’s decree.

As stated by Fakhr al-Rāzī in his commentary on it: ‘Know that God has already determined that some of the people of the Day of Resurrection are felicitous and others are wretched. If God has decreed thus, then it is impossible for it to be otherwise. Otherwise, it would mean that God’s statement is false and His knowledge is ignorance, which is impossible. Therefore, it is established that the felicitous person does not turn into a wretched one, and the wretched person does not turn into a felicitous one.’ He further narrates a report that says ʿUmar asked the Prophet after the revelation of the verse, Some of them will be wretched and some felicitous: ‘O Messenger of God, then why should we do anything? For something already predetermined or for something yet to be decided?’ The

Prophet replied, ‘For something already settled, ʿUmar. The pens have been lifted, and the scrolls have dried up, yet everyone will find it easy to do that for which they were created.’ Al-Raẓi continues: ‘The M uʿtazila say, citing a report from al-Ḥasan: “Among them, some are wretched due to their deeds and others are happy due to their deeds.” We argue that these reports cannot refute the decisive evidence (al-dalīl al-qāṭiʿ) we have already presented.

Furthermore, there is no dispute that an individual is miserable due to his deeds and happy due to his deeds. But because these actions occurred by the decree and predestination of God, the argument we have presented remains valid.’

One of the extraordinary fallacies in this argument lies in what al-Rāzī terms ‘decisive evidence.’ There is an error in taking the time of the judgement as the time for its result and effect. It is obvious that a truthful judgement now about attributing a characteristic to a subject at a future time

does not entail this attribution except at that future time, not at the time when the judge makes the judgement, which is now. For instance, our judgement that at night that the sky will grow brighter in a few hours—a true judgement—does not necessitate the sky being light at night when we make that judgement. Equally, our judgement that a boy will become an old man in eighty years does not require him to be an old man at the time of the judgement.

So when God says, Some of them will be wretched and some felicitous, God is informing us that a group of them will be wretched on the Day of Resurrection and others will be felicitous on the Day of Resurrection. If this is a judgement about their wretchedness and felicitousness, then it is a judgement made by Him now that they will be one or the other in future, on the Day of Resurrection. And it is assumed that this judgement will not change from what it is in its context, otherwise, it would mean that God’s information is false and His knowledge is ignorance. However, this is not a judgement made by Him now that they are either wretched or felicitous now, or a judgement made by Him now that they are either wretched or felicitous permanently. This is self-evident.

After all, if al-Rāzī actually believes this, then what prevented him from making such a claim regarding everything that God Almighty has informed us about people’s characteristics on the Day of Resurrection. W hy not judge them as being either eternally believers or disbelievers, or being in Paradise before the Day of Resurrection, and in Hell before the Day of Resurrection? This is because his evidence applies equally to these and other cases, such as wretchedness and felicitousness.

As for the narration cited by al-Rāzī, in which the Prophet says, ‘… yet everyone will find it easy to do what they were created for’, this has no relevance to what he mentioned in the first place. A clarification of this will come in our explanation of the narrations.

Finally, when al-Rāzī says, ‘there is no dispute that an individual is miserable due to his deeds and happy due to his deeds. But because these actions occurred by the decree and predestination of God, the argument we have presented remains valid’, he means that the divine decree’s attachment to action necessitates its permanence. This would mean that the action is forced upon the person, not a choice in which with the performance or non-performance of the act are both equally possible for the person, and that they had no say in it and no influence on the action in bringing about wretchedness or felicitousness. In fact, according to this model, there is a purely coincidental association between the person and the action, and between the action and the consequence of either misery or happiness. In other words, all of these elements are linked merely by virtue of God’s placing one thing after another, without any real causal connection between

them or any influence on one another.

This is another fallacy arising from the confusion between the attribute of necessity and the attribute of contingency. The action has a sufficient cause (ʿilla tāmma) that necessitates its existence, such as the combination of the human will, the readiness of the means of action, the existence of material receptive to action, time, place, and the absence of obstacles and impediments, among other things. When all of these factors are gathered together, completed, and fulfilled, there exists a sufficient cause and the action’s occurrence becomes an ontological necessity. Thus, the action has the attribute of necessity in relation its sufficient cause as a whole and the attribute of contingency in relation to each part of its sufficient cause, including the human will.

The action that is realized by the necessity of the sufficient cause, at this moment, has the attribute of necessity in relation to the sum of the sufficient cause (whose constituent factors are detailed above), and an attribute of contingency to the human will. The attribute of the action’s necessity in relation to the sufficient cause does not negate its attribute of contingency in relation to the human will (which is a necessary cause, but not a sufficient one by itself), nor does it shift it from possibility to actuality. Rather, the action’s relationship to the human being is always one

of contingency, just as its relationship to the sum of the human and the other components of the sufficient cause is always one of necessity. The two possibilities of the performance and non-performance of an action are always equal with respect to the human being, just as one of the two possibilities of performance and non-performance is always determined with consideration to the sufficient cause.

Hence, we can conclude that human actions are voluntary in essence, as their existence cannot be devoid of a sufficient cause. The irrevocable divine decree is one of God’s active attributes, which are abstracted from the station of action, which is a chain of causes arranged according to the cosmic order. Now, the ontological necessity of effects in relation to their causes, or that of every decreed thing in relation to its divine decree, does not contradict its voluntary nature of actions for human beings, and the relation of actions to human beings is one of contingency. Al-Rāzī has understood the relation of an act to human beings as one of ontological necessity rather than contingency, by assuming that an action being necessitated by the divine decree entails the necessity of its occurrence in relation

to humans, rather than its mere contingency.

To put it another way, suppose that God had knowledge that a certain piece of wood will burn in fire, does this entail that the wood will

necessarily combust, regardless of whether there is fire? No, because the truth of God’s knowledge depends on the wood being burnt by fire, not it burning regardless of external factors. Similarly, God’s knowledge that a human will perform a certain act out of his or her own free will and volition, or that he or she will suffer a certain consequence due to a voluntary

action he or she has performed, necessitates the inevitability of the action through human choice, not the inevitability of a certain action regardless of whether the human being chooses to do it or not, or whether there is a human being or not, which would sever the causal connection between the human and their action. Therefore, God’s knowledge that a particular human being will suffer due to their own voluntary disbelief necessitates the suffering caused by their disbelief, not suffering regardless of whether there is disbelief or not.

Hence, it is clear that God’s knowledge of human action does not necessitate the nullification of free will or the affirmation of predestination, even though His knowledge does not deviate from His decree, and

there is no way to repel His decree.

(11:106) As for the wretched, they shall be in the Fire: their lot therein will be groaning and wailing (zafīr wa shahīq).

In M ajmaʿ al-bayān, al-Ṭabrisī writes: “Zafīr denotes the beginning of a donkey’s braying, and shahīq denotes the end of it.”

In al-Kashshāf, al-Zamakhsharī writes: “Zafīr means the exhalation of breath, while shahīq means its inhalation.”

In his M ufradāt, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī says: “Zafīr refers to inhalation that causes the ribs to expand noticeably … shahīq is the prolongation of this. Therefore, together zafīr and shahīq denote taking violent breaths in-and-out. God says, their lot therein will bezafīr wa shahīq;they will hear it raging and roaring (zafīr) (25:12), and they hear it blaring, as it seethes

(67:7), and the root of the word shahīq is from shāhiq, which means ‘a towering mountain.”’

As you can see, the meanings of zafīr and shahīq are very close to one another, and the verse here is using them figuratively. The intended meaning is that the wretched will suck air into to their lungs, then exhale it, lengthening their cries and groans due to the severe heat of the fire and the magnitude of the disaster and misfortune they have suffered, producing a sound similar to that made by a donkey when it brays.

At first glance, it seems that following from the statement, Some of them will be wretched and some felicitous, the present verse should have read: ‘As for he who is miserable (singular), he is in the fire, and in it he has gasping and panting.’ However, the prior context which opened with a description of the Day of Judgement, That is a day for which all mankind will be

gathered, and it is a day witnessed,which emphasized the fact that there would be a multitude of people gathered together. The implication of this is that there will be groups on that day: those who are miserable and those who are happy. Now, in the previous verse, God uses the term wretched (shaqī) and felicitous (saʿīd) in the singular and indefinite form because the prior expression in the same verse, no one shall speak except by His leave, also uses the singular indefinite form to convey the comprehensiveness of tis negation. However, once that aim has been achieved in the full verse, The day it comes, no one shall speak except by His leave. Some of them will be wretched and some felicitous, the discourse returns to using the plural form for the next three verses to emphasize the fact that there are many people gathered together: As for the wretched …

(11:107) They shall remain in it (khālidīn fī-hā) for as long as the heavens and the earth endure—except what your Lord may wish; indeed your Lord does what He desires.

This expounds the term that the inhabitants of Hell will serve therein, paralleling the following verse, As for the felicitous, they will be in paradise. They will remain in it (khālidīn fī-hā) for as long as the heavens and the earth endure—except what your Lord may wish—an endless bounty (11:108), which explains the term that the inhabitants of Paradise will dwell therein, and this supports the notion that both groups will reside permanently in these abodes.

Al-Rāghib says in his Mufradāt:

“Khulūd (from whence khālidīn is derived) means for something to endure without being afiected by corruption, and its remaining in the condition it is in. Anything that change and corruption are slow to effect, the Arabs describe as khālid, which is why they call stones used around their cooking fires khawālid. However, this is due to their long-lasting existence, not because they are genuinely perpetual or eternal. God says, You set up structures as if you will be immortal (takhludūn) (26:129).”

The term khald refers to whatever part of the human being remains unchanged so long as they are alive, unlike the rest of his parts. The original meaning of the term mukhallad, is something that endures for a long

time—for example, a rajul mukhallad, is a man who appears slow to show signs of ageing, or a dāba mukhallada, is an animal which does not lose all of its second set of teeth until its fourth set begin to show. Then, this came to be used metaphorically for something that endures eternally.’

Eternity in Paradise refers to the persistence of things in the state they are in without being afiected by corruption. God says, they shall be the inhabitants of paradise; they shall remain in it (hum fī-hā khālidūn) (2:82); such shall be the inmates of the Fire, and they shall remain in it (2:81); Should anyone kill a believer intentionally, his requital shall be hell, to remain therein (khālidan fī-hā) (4:93).

Elsewhere, God says, They will be waited upon by immortal youths (wildān mukhalladūn) (76:19). It is said that mukhallad here means these youths will remain in their young state without ageing. Another interpretation states that it means they will be wearing a type of anklet called khulda.

The verb ikhlād means to make something last or believe that it will endure. Therefore, the verse, but he clung to the earth (wa lakinna-hu akhlada ilā al-arḍ) means that he relied upon the earth because he believed he would live on it eternally.

The phrase, as long as the heavens and the earth endure, is a phrase that qualifies the statement, they shall remain in it, in a way that emphasizes the meaning of perpetuity. The implication is that they will remain in that state for as long as the heavens and earth continue to exist. However, other verses of the Qur’an explicitly state that the heavens and earth will not endure eternally, while others still affirm that both Heaven and Hell will continue to exist without ending or fading.

Verses that affirm the former include: We did not create the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them except with reason and for a specified term (46:3); The day W e shall roll up the sky, like the rolling of the scrolls for writings. W e will bring it back as W e began the first creation—a promise binding on Us. That indeed We will do (21:104); … yet the entire earth will be in His fist on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens, scrolled, in His right hand (39:67); And: W hen the earth is shaken violently, and the mountains are shattered into bits and become scattered dust (56:4–6). Verses that affirm the latter include: … gardens with streams running in them, to remain in them forever. That is the great success. (64:9); Indeed Allah has cursed the faithless and prepared for them a blaze, in which they will remain forever. They will not find any guardian or helper (33:64–65). Therefore, two issues arise out two verses:

The first is the fact that they connect their perpetuity to the persistence of the heavens and the earth, which is not perpetual according to

the above cited verses.

The second issue is that it links the eternal reality that begins on the Day of Resurrection—the fact that the two groups are in Heaven and Hell and destined to remain therein— with something whose existence ends on the Day of Resurrection—the heavens and the earth.

This second issue is more problematic than the first because it is relevant even to those who do not believe in eternity in either Hell or both

Heaven and Hell, unlike the first issue.

The resolution to this dilemma lies in the fact that God, in His Book, mentions that in the Hereafter there are an earth and heavens, even if they differ from what we know in this world. God says, The day the earth is transformed into another earth and the heavens, and they are presented before Allah, the One, the All-paramount (14:48). He also states, relating the words of the inhabitants of Paradise, They will say, ‘All praise belongs to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us and made us heirs to the earth, that we may settle in paradise wherever we may wish!’ How excellent is the reward of the workers (39:74).And He describes the believers, saying, For such will be the reward of the ultimate abode (13:22).

Thus, the Hereafter has its heavens and earth, just as it has a Heaven and Hell, each with its own inhabitants. God the Sublime describes all of these as being with Him, stating, That which is with you will be spent but what is with Allah shall last (16:96). With these words, He decrees that they are everlasting and not fieeting.

God links the permanence of Heaven and Hell and their inhabitants to the persistence of the heavens and earth because the heavens and earth, in their general sense (in that they will be transformed into a new heavens and a new earth in the hereafter), are eternal and not transient. However, these heavens and earth that we experience in this world will come to an end based on the observable order. As for the heavens that shade Heaven, for instance, and the earth that carries it, which are illuminated by the light of their Lord, they are permanent and never fading. The universe will never be devoid of them. In this way, both of the aforementioned dilemmas are resolved.

In Tafsīr al-Kashshāf, al-Zamahsharī alludes to this perspective, saying: “The evidence that there are heavens and earth in the Hereafter is

His saying, The day the earth is transformed into another earth and the heavens (14:48) and His saying, and made us heirs to the earth, that we may settle in paradise wherever we may wish (39:74). This is because the land of the Hereafter must have something beneath it and something above it, either a heaven that God creates or the Divine Throne that overshadows it. Anything that overshadows something else can be referred to as a samāʾ.” However, the second perspective al-Zamakhsharī mentions appears nonsensical, as it establishes the existence of the heavens and earth in relative terms, namely that both Heaven and Hell must conceptually have an

‘above’ and a ‘below.’ Thus, Paradise and Hell are primary in existence, while their heavens and earth are secondary. According to this conceptualization, the permanence of their heavens and earth is determined by the

permanence of Paradise and Hell, not the reverse, which is what is indicated in the verse. This perspective necessitates that Heaven and Hell must have an earth beneath and a heaven above them. However, regarding the heavens in the plural form (samāwāt), as in the verse, this argument does not apply, leaving the complication regarding the heavens unresolved.

The above refutes the explanation given by al-Qāḍī al-Bayḍāwī1 in his commentary, in which he says: “This point of view is problematic because it draws a comparison with something that most of creation does not recognise in terms of its existence and permanence. And for those who recognise it, they understand it only in terms of the continuation of reward

and punishment, so the analogy doesn’t hold value for them.”

What he means by this is that the verse draws a parallel between the permanence of Paradise and Hell and their inhabitants with the persistence
