Ashaʿrī theological school, and a commentator of the Qurʾān. His commentary, Anwār al-tanzīl wa-asrār al-taʾwīl was one of the most popular commentaries in the pre-modern Sunnī world. The Shīʿī scholar Fayḍ Kāshānī also refers to it in his commentaries on the Qur’an, al-Ṣāfī and al-Aṣfā.

of the heavens and the earth. If the heavens and earth in the verse refer to those of the Hereafter, and most of the creation doesn’t recognise their existence and permanence, then this analogy would be trying to explain what is clear by comparing it to something obscure, which violates the rules of rhetoric.

To this I respond: We only understood the permanence of Paradise and Hell and their inhabitants from the words of God, just as we have understood the existence of a heavens and an earth for them and the eternity of

all of these from His words. So, what prevents someone from defining one revealed truth in His words in terms of another found in His words, especially if one truth is better known among the people than the other after

both have been taken from His words and not from an external source? This also refutes what al-Ālūsī has said concerning the same topic, that what comes to mind from the heavens and the earth are the familiar celestial bodies we know and that, therefore, it is more fitting to seek another

explanation for the verse other than the one presented.

The reason what we have said refutes al-Ālūsī’s statement is that the meanings of Qur’anic verses are based on the understanding of competent speakers of the language concerning the general connotations that

are conveyed by the lexical meaning (lugha) and common usage (ʿurf) of words. However, regarding the specific intents and the particular realities upon which these connotations operate, this is not the case. Instead, the preferred approach is to contemplate upon the Qur’an (tadabbur), which God has commanded, and returning the ambiguous verses to the clear ones, and comparing one verse with another, because the Qur’an confirms some parts of itself with others, and some parts speak, prove, and validate the others, as we find in the traditions. Hence, when we hear God describe Himself as ‘One, Unique, Omniscient, Omnipotent, Living, Willing, Hearing, and Seeing’ or other attributes, we should not understand them based merely on the apparent meanings determined by the common usage of the Arabic language, but based on what the very words of God explain and what deep contemplation reveals to us about their meanings. We have already discussed this in our discourse on the clear and ambiguous verses in our commentary on Sūrah Āl ʿImrān.

Other explanations of the verse have been offered in various traditions and in the commentaries of other exegetes. We will detail what we have found of these here, following on from the first explanation, given above. The second explanation is that what is meant by the heavens are the heavens of Paradise and Hell and their earth— meaning whatever it is that shades them and whatever it is they rest upon. Anything that is above and shades them is considered a heaven (samāʾ), and whatever your foot rests upon is considered an earth (arḍ). In other words, what is meant is whatever is above them and what is below them.

This is the explanation that al-Zamakhsharī proposed at the end of the section of his commentary we quoted above, and the reader is aware of the problems inherent in it, as this explanation does not make clear why the term ‘heavens’ (samāwāt) is mentioned in plural in the verse, rather than the singular, as we have already noted.

The third explanation is that as long as the heavens and the earth endure means ‘as long as the Hereafter exists,’ and it is eternal, just as the permanence of the heavens and the earth in this life is determined by the extent

of their lifespan. Perhaps the intended meaning of the phrase as long as the heavens and the earth endure is a as a simile, just as one might say, ‘He spoke the words of one who mocks’, meaning he spoke in the same manner as those who mock and ridicule.

However, if this sort of simile was what was intended by the verse, it would convey the opposite of the desired meaning, which is impermanence. And if something other than this was intended, the phrasing of

the verse would not suffice.

The fourth explanation is that it the phrase is intended to convey the meaning of ‘a very long time’— in the sense of eternity— rather than to actually specify the duration of the heavens and the earth’s existence. The Arabs have numerous expressions they use to convey perpetuity, without meaning the literal sense of those expressions. For example, they would say, ‘The matter will remain thus, as long as night and day continue to alternate,’ or ‘as long as the east wind blows,’ or ‘as long as stars rise,’ or ‘as long as breezes blow,’ or ‘as long as the heavens exist.’ They turned to these phrases, assuming that these things are eternal and unending. They then used them as if they were coined to convey the idea of perpetuity. However, the problem with this explanation is that the Arabs only used these expressions to convey the meaning of eternity— and frequently did so— because they believed these phenomena were indeed eternal. On the other hand, if there is someone who explicitly states that they have a limited and finite existence and believes that considering them as only existing temporarily is an essential doctrine of faith, then it is inappropriate for such a person to employ such phrases to convey the meaning of

eternity, no matter the context. How could it be otherwise when God has said, We did not create the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them except with reason and for a specified term (46:3)? How then could it be correct to say that heaven and hell will exist eternally ‘as long as the heavens and the earth endure’?

The fifth explanation is that it means they will live so long as the heavens and the earth (whose end is known) endure, after which God will

extend their existence, granting them eternal life and perpetuating their state. This is akin to saying, ‘They will live for such-and-such number of years,’ after which God adds to that an immeasurable span of time, as in the verse, to reside therein for ages (78:23), meaning they will live for ages, and then they will be given an even longer term than that.

However, the problem with this perspective is that it appears to be based on interpreting some phrases, such as, ‘as long as the heavens and the earth endure’ as denoting a specified period of time, while reading others, such as, ‘except what your Lord may wish,’ as signifying a limitless duration. However, such an explanation requires the reader to make assumptions that have no basis whatsoever in the text itself.

The sixth explanation is that the reference to Paradise and Hell in this verse is to the paradise and hell of the intermediate realm (Barzakh). In other words, these will endure as long as the heavens and the earth endure. When the duration of the heavens and the earth comes to an end with the Day of Resurrection, people will be brought out of this temporary paradise and temporary hell and mustered for final judgement.

However, this reading does not accord with the context of the verses, which start by mentioning the Day of Resurrection and describing it with certain attributes. This discourse begins by mentioning ‘a day for which all mankind will be gathered’ and ‘a day witnessed’ on which ‘no one shall speak except by His leave’, and then highlights its most specific and distinctive qualities, namely the clear descriptions of reward and punishment in

the eternal Paradise and Hell. Therefore, it is highly unlikely that, after all of this, such a discourse would then divert to discussing the temporary paradise and hell of the intermediate realm.

In addition to this, God describes the punishment of Barzakh as being exposed to the Fire, not entering it: the Fire, to which they are exposed morning and evening. And on the day when the Hour sets in Pharaoh’s clan will

enter the severest punishment (40:46).

The seventh explanation is that entering Hellfire in his verse refers to being under the influence of Satan, while being in Paradise refers to being under the guardianship of God. This is because God’s guardianship is made manifest in the Paradise of the Hereafter, in which the felicitous receive His blessings. By contrast, Satan’s influence becomes tangible in the form of the flames of Hell, in which the wrongdoers are tormented on the Day of Resurrection. This is supported by those verses that discuss the tangible manifestation of people’s deeds in the afterlife (tajassum al-aʿmāl). Therefore, the wretched enter Hell because of their wretchedness, but they might be taken out of it if they receive God’s blessings and grace, like a disbeliever who believes after his disbelief or a criminal who repents. Equally, the felicitous enter Paradise due to their felicitousness, but they might be led astray by Satan to cling to worldly desires, and follow their whims, like a believer who becomes a disbeliever or a righteous person who turns corrupt.

However, the problem with this reading is the same as what has already been mentioned, namely that it goes against the grain of this section of verses. These verses detail the unique, awe-inspiring, and astounding attributes of the Day of Resurrection that melt hearts and boggle minds upon

hearing and reflecting upon them. They serve as a warning to the arrogant and deniers among the disbelievers and act as a deterrent for the sinful. Therefore, it is highly improbable that the verses would mention that it is a day when all people are gathered, a witnessed day, and a day in which no one speaks unless permitted, and then mention that the disbelievers and sinners are in Hellfire from the moment they disbelieved and sinned until the Day of Judgement, and that the believers and those who perform righteous deeds are in Paradise from the moment they believed and acted righteously. Firstly, this account doesn’t fit the context because the verses describe the unique features of the Day of Judgement, not what precedes and leads to it. Secondly, the verses are intended as warnings and glad tidings. Such concealed truths would not concern the arrogant and tyrannical

disbelievers; they would not value them, nor would they be deterred by fear of such misery or hope for such spiritual happiness, as should be obvious. However, this interpretation is still valid within the deeper layers of

the Qur’an’s meaning.

There are still other explanations of the verse, which revolve around the phrase, except what your Lord may wish, whose discussion we have eschewed here for the sake of brevity. They share common problems with the explanations proposed for this phrase, which we will detail below. God’s statement, except what (mā) your Lord may wish, is an exception to what was previously mentioned about the wretched dwelling eternally in the fire. It corresponds to the statement following the mention of the felicitous dwelling eternally in Paradise. The word mā in ‘what your Lord may wish’ is commonly understood as being an infinitive modifier, which shifts the meaning of the phrase thus: ‘unless your Lord wishes that they do not dwell therein eternally.’ However, this reading is undermined by the subsequent phrase, indeed your Lord does what (mā) He desires,where mā is used as a relative pronoun (in the sense of ‘whatever’), and the meanings of ‘what your Lord may wish’ and ‘what He desires’ should be one and

the same.

Alternatively, the word mā in except what your Lord may wish can be a relative pronoun, signifying an exception to the duration that is understood from the context to be perpetual. This means that they will dwell in

it for all future times, perpetually, except for what your Lord may wish. Or, the exception might relate to the collective pronoun in they shall remain in it. This means all of them will dwell therein except those whom God wills to remove from Hell and admit to Paradise. This aligns with reports that sinful and disobedient believers will not remain in Hellfire forever; they will eventually leave and enter Paradise due on account of receiving intercession. The exit of some people from Hellfire at a future time is sufficient to both preserve the general meaning of the verb while maintaining

the validity of the exception.

One point that must addressed in this case is that the verse uses the relative pronoun mā (‘what’) to refer to rational beings (when it is commonly used for non-rational beings). However, there is no problem with

this, even if it is not commonplace. We can find other examples of this usage in the Qur’an. For example: … then marry such women as you like … (4:3). The explanation of the following verse, As for the felicitous … (11:108), parallels that of the present one, as they both share the same context and structure. However, the exception, except what your Lord may wish, in the verse about Paradise is followed by the clause, an endless bounty. This indicates that the exception here does not concern the certainty that they will dwell in Paradise forever, as such an exception would not cohere with the fact that the reward of Paradise is an unending gift. On the contrary, it only points to the mere possibility of occurrence. Therefore, the meaning is: ‘the people of Paradise will be there forever, unless God removes them from it. But the gift of Paradise is everlasting, and they will never leave, because God would never will such a thing!’

Thus, this exception serves to safeguard God’s omnipotence. Indeed, God’s power over them is not depleted by His admitting them to Paradise, His sovereignty is not nullified, and His kingdom does not fade. His omnipotence and control over time remains as they were before. To Him belongs the power to remove them from Paradise, despite His promise that they will dwell there permanently. However, He will not remove them due to this promise, for God does not break His promises.

Now, the discussion of the exception in the present verse (11:107), meaning the verse of Hellfire, is identical to that of the exception in the verse of Paradise, given the shared context and obvious parallels between the two verses in terms of structure. However, the difference is that God follows the exception of this verse with the phrase, indeed your Lord does what He desires, which carries an obvious indication that whatever He wills will certainly transpire.

Therefore, the inmates of the Fire, like the inhabitants of Paradise, will never leave, unless God wills so, because He is capable of all things. No action of His, whether conferring or withholding, can entail the negation of His power or the situation getting out of His control, for His power is absolute, unbound by any limitation, nor prevented from accomplishing one thing by another. He said, and Allah does whatever He wishes (14:27) and Allah effaces and confirms whatever He wishes (13:39), among other verses.

There is no contradiction between this explanation and what is narrated in the reports about some of the guilty being removed from the Fire

by God’s will, as should be clear.

This is one explanation of the exception, and there are other interpretations that are collectively summarized in M ajmaʿ al-bayān, up to ten.

What we have outlined here is only the first of these.

The second explanation of the exception posits that it refers to an increase in punishment for the inhabitants of Hell and an increase in bliss for the inhabitants of Heaven. Thus, except what your Lord may wish could be understood signifying an increase beyond the established degree, just as a man might say to another, ‘I owe you a thousand dinars, except (illā) for the two thousand that I loaned you at a particular time.’ In this case, the two thousand would indeed be an addition to the original thousand. Here, the exception signified by the preposition illā takes the meaning of ‘in addition to’, as in ‘in addition to what your Lord wills’, akin to the phrase, ‘No man was with us except Zaid’, meaning ‘in addition to Zaid.’ This view is built on the premise that God’s statement, as long as the heavens and the earth endure, does not imply perpetuity or eternity, and the reader is already are of the arguments against this.

The third explanation is that the exception refers to their status at the place of Resurrection, as they are neither in Heaven nor in Hell, but rather in a state of limbo, known as the Isthmus (Barzakh), which lies between death and resurrection. For, if God had said ‘they will abide therein forever’, without making an exception, one might assume they would be in

Hell or Heaven from the moment the verse was revealed or after their time of moral responsibility comes to an end. Thus, the exception serves a purpose here.

If it one was to ask, ‘How can an exception be made from their dwelling eternally in Hell before they have even entered it?’, the answer is that

it is possible if this announcement is made prior to their entering it. However, this interpretation has no basis in the wording of the verse, and it appears to be based on reading the previous statement, some of them will be wretched and some felicitous, as being an affirmation of some people being predestined to be wretched and others to be felicitous, without them having any free will or moral choice in the matter. The fallacy of such a reading should be obvious.

The fourth explanation sees the first of the two exceptions as connected to His saying, their lot therein will be groaning and wailing. Here, except what your Lord may wish, is assumed to refer to forms of punishment other than these two types, with the exception not relating to the eternal duration of the punishment. Equally, for the inhabitants of Heaven, it is connected to an implicit corresponding meaning. It is as if God had said, ‘They will have such a blessing therein, except what your Lord wills of other types of blessings.’ This interpretation is implied by His saying, an endless bounty. However, this reading assumes that the two exceptions belong to different contexts without any evidence for this. This is evident in the fact

that it understands the first exception to mean ‘in addition to’, while it understands the second exception as a genuine exception. However, there is no evidence that the first exception is related to his saying their lot therein will be groaning and wailing, nor that an endless bounty implies what proponents of this reading claim. The latter verse only indicates the perpetuity of the gift, without specifying whether this means all types of gifts or only some of them.

Subsequently, one may inquire about the utility of distinguishing some types of blessings in paradise and exposing this to the listeners, given that the context is one of assurance and joyful news, and the circumstance is one of invitation and encouragement. This is among the most absurd aspects of the reading.

The fifth explanation is that illā (‘except’) means ‘and’, otherwise, the discourse would be self-contradictory. Therefore, the meaning of the phrases would be: ‘they will dwell therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, and as your Lord wills in addition to this.’

However, it has not been established that the particle illā can indeed be read with the meaning of ‘and.’ Indeed, this is something that has only been mentioned by the medieval grammarian al-Farrāʾ, and it is an opinion that experts have considered weak. Furthermore, this reading is baed on the assumption that the phrase, as long as the heavens and the earth endure, does not convey the meaning of eternity or perpetuity, and the reader is already familiar with the debates concerning this.

The sixth explanation is that the wretched refers to those monotheists who have been consigned to Hellfire. They are those who have combined belief and obedience with acts of disobedience that necessitate their

imprisonment in Hell. Therefore, God Almighty has said that they will be punished in Hellfire except what your Lord may wish, namely except when God removes them from it to take them to Heaven and reward them for their acts of obedience.

As for the exception for the inhabitants of Paradise, it is an exception that applies to those monotheists who have been released from Hell and admitted to Paradise, because anyone transferred from Hell to Paradise and granted eternal life therein must be described as dwelling there eternally, but with an exception because they were elsewhere before they arrived. It is as if to say: ‘they are in Paradise, and they will dwell therein forever, except what your Lord willed concerning the time they were consigned to Hell.’ According to the proponents of this reading, the wretched ones are identical with the felicitous ones, and both designations apply to them depending on their situation. When they are cast into Hell and punished therein, they are the wretched ones. However, when they are admitted to Paradise a granted its blessings, they are the felicitous ones. This explanation is attributed to the Companions Ibn ʿAbbās, Jābir b. ʿAbd Allāh, and

Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, as well as a group of the Successors.

However, this reading does not accord with the context, because God Almighty, after describing the Day of Resurrection as a day when people are gathered together, divided the people who will be gathered into two groups with his statement: Some of them will be wretched and some felicitous. It is obvious that his statement, As for the wretched …, and his statement, As for the felicitous …, each introduce a separate point, as evinced by

the fact they begin with the prepositional phrase ‘as for’ (fa ammā), which indicates that what follows it is an exposition of the statement, Some of them will be wretched and some felicitous. Therefore, based on the fact that this statement is an exhaustive division of all the people gathered on the Day of Resurrection, this means that the wretched are all of the people of Hell, and not merely a particular group of them, and the felicitous are all the people of Paradise, and not only those who were freed from Hell and admitted to Paradise.

That is, unless one were to say that the phrase, Some of them will be wretched and some felicitous, is also a description of a specific group in the same vein as they claim that the phrases, the wretched and the felicitous, both refer to the same group. Read like this, the verse’s meaning becomes: ‘Some of those gathered on the Day of Resurrection will be both wretched and felicitous, and they are the ones who will be consigned to Hell and abide therein so long as the heavens and the earth endure, except when your Lord wishes to bring them out from it, admit them to Paradise, make them felicitous therein, and cause them to dwell therein for as long as the heavens and earth endure, except for the time when they were wretched aforehand and dwelt in Hell before entering paradise.’

However, the problem we raised earlier would then apply to the purported meaning of His saying, Some of them will be wretched and some

felicitous. The apparent context, which portrays the gathering of humankind as a whole on the Day of Resurrection, does not support the idea

that His saying, Some of them will be wretched and some felicitous, refers to a specific group of people. As this would mean that this single group are then apparently divided into two groups to describe their situation while remaining a single group in essence, and presenting them in the form of two separate subjects for two separate categories, with two specific references to the endurance of the heavens and earth, followed by two separate

exceptions that are intended to represent only one. If this were indeed what was meant by the verse, then what is the benefit of such a specification, when it leads to so much unnecessary ambiguity and complexity in

the wording of the verses?

One could also argue for this reading by appealing to a more general meaning. For example, one might say that the phrase, Some of them will be wretched and some felicitous, is a general division of humanity on the Day of Judgement into those who are wretched and those who are felicitous, while As for the wretched … refers to the people of Hell, and As for

the felicitous … refers to the inhabitants of Paradise, while the exception in both instances refers to the sinful monotheists, who God will take out of the Fire and admit to Paradise. In this way, most of the problems that arose against the previous standpoint are resolved.

The seventh explanation is that invoking the contingency of this on the Divine Will is actually to emphasize that the inhabitants of Hell and Paradise will dwell in each eternally and make the prospect of them ever exiting these seem distant, because God does not will anything other than their perpetuity and eternity, which He has ordained. It is as if this is contingent on what will not be, because He does not will to take them out

of either.

This reading shares in common with the first one the claim that the exception in both instances is not intended to negate the eternal duration of Paradise and Hell. However, the first reading makes the specific claim that the exception is to safeguard God’s omnipotence, while this explanation makes the specific claim that the exception is to demonstrate that eternity cannot be disrupted by any means, unless God wills to disrupt it, and He will not will that in the first place.

The eighth explanation is that what is intended here is the exception of the time when a group from the inhabitants of Hell entered before another group, and the same in the case of groups who enter Heaven. God Almighty says elsewhere, The faithless will be driven to hell in throngs … Those who are wary of their Lord will be led to paradise in throngs (39:71). Thus, one group of them among them enters after another, and there must be a delay between the two of them. According to this explanation, it is this that God is excluding when He says, except what your Lord may wish. This explanation has been transmitted from Salām b. al-M ustanīr al-Basrī. However, the problem with this explanation is that the phrase, They shall remain in it for as long as the heavens and the earth endure, in both the case of Hell and of Paradise, is that this description appears to concern the length of their stay in each from the aspect of its ending point rather than its starting point.

In any case, the beginning of the duration of their imprisonment in Hell or inhabitation of Paradise is the Day of Judgement, and this is not afiected because one group enters Paradise or Hell after another group or before it and the time difference that results from that.

The ninth explanation is that what is meant is that they will dwell in Hell, being tormented therein for the duration of their existence in the graves as long as the heavens and the earth last in this world. When they perish and cease to exist, their punishment will be interrupted until God resurrects them for the Final Judgement. God’s saying, except what your Lord may wish, is an exception that applies to what will happen in the Hereafter. This interpretation has been reported in M ajmaʿ al-bayān from Shaykh Abū Jaʿfar al-Ṭūsī in his own Tafsīr, quoting from a number of Shīʿī scholars in their own commentaries.

However, the issue with this explanation is the same as that of the second one, which is based on taking the particle illā to mean ‘aside from’,

and the reader will already be familiar with the problems inherent in this. The tenth explanation is that what is meant by except what your Lord may wish is ‘whoever your Lord wishes to forgive and hence will not let them enter Hell.’ Therefore, the exception is from the pronoun that refers back to As for the wretched. The apparent meaning of the exception God directs towards the inhabitants of Paradise in the passage, As for the felicitous, … except what your Lord may wish, refers to the monotheists who come

out of Hell and are admitted to Paradise, as has already been mentioned in some of the previous points. The meaning is that the felicitous ones are in Heaven, dwelling therein eternally, except for the transgressors from the monotheists who are in Hell and then they are brought of there and lodged in Paradise. This explanation has been attributed to Abū M ajāz. However, what has been stated applies only to the first exception; the second exception must necessarily be directed in a different way, which in any case would necessarily disrupt the unity of the context that exists between the two verses.

Consider that sinners among the faithful, whom God forgives and thereby does not send to Hell, are not pardoned unconditionally, but rather are forgiven due to good deeds they performed or the intercession of others on their behalf. Thus, they become blessed and are included in the second verse: As for the felicitous, they will be in paradise …, without first being included among the wretched and then being exempted from entering hell. In short, they are not wretched to be exempted; rather, they are felicitous and will enter paradise from the beginning.

… indeed your Lord does what He desires— serves as a rationale for the exception while simultaneously affirming God’s omnipotence through its unrestricted meaning, as previously mentioned.

(11:108) As for the felicitous, they will be in paradise. They will remain in it for as long as the heavens and the earth endure— except what your Lord may wish—an endless bounty (ʿaṭāʾan ghayr majdhūdh).

This can be read in one of two ways: the passive voice (‘those who are made felicitous’) and in the active voice (‘those who are felicitous’). The latter seems more linguistically appropriate because the verb saʿāda is intransitive in everyday usage. However, reading the felicitous in the passive voice, while reading the wretched in the previous verse in the active

voice, subtly implies that happiness and goodness come from God, while the evil that afflicts them is self-imposed, as stated in Sūrah al-Nūr (24:21): Were it not for Allah’s grace and His mercy upon you, not one of you would ever be pure.

The adjective majdhūdh is derived from jadhdh, meaning ‘to cut of .’ Therefore, describing God’s gift as ghayr majdhūdh means that it is never cut of  and never ends. In other words, Paradise is a never-ending divine gift, in spite of the previous exception of except what your Lord may wish. This is one of the most beautiful indications that the purpose behind this exception is to affirm God’s absolute omnipotence and sovereignty and show that the reins of power are never out of his His hands.

Everything that was discussed in relation to the preceding verse applies to the present verse, except for the explanations based on the assumption that the exception in His statement, except what your Lord may wish, refers to those who first entered Hell and then moved to Paradise. That is because it is possible for some who enters Hell to later exit it, but no one who enters Paradise, which is the eternal Paradise, will ever exit it as a form of otherworldy punishment. This is an essential principle that is established in the Qur’an and traditions. There is such an abundance of verses and narrations in this regard that no one can possibly deny their implication, even

if the Qur’an’s statements about some people leaving hell are not as clear. In M ajmaʿ al-bayān, al-Tabrisī says about the necessity of the virtuous entering Paradise and the impossibility of them ever leaving it: ‘It is a

consensus of the Muslim community that whoever deserves divine reward must enter Paradise and that He will never leave it after He has entered it.’ The idea that those people worthy of divine reward must necessarily enter Paradise is based on the universally accepted rational principle that fulfilling a promise is obligatory, unlike fulfilling a threat. This is because the one to whom promise is made is conferred a right to what is promise, and not fulfilling this promise equates to neglecting another’s right, which is an act of injustice. As for the threat, it is making a right for the issuer to act against the person to whom the threat is made. It is not obligatory for the holder of the right to claim his right, but he may choose to do so or to forgo it. God, the Glorious, has promised His obedient servants Paradise as a reward for their obedience, and He has threatened the disobedient with Hell for their disobedience. Therefore, it is obligatory that the obedient enter Paradise in fulfilment of the right that He has made incumbent for them upon Himself. As for the punishment of the disobedient, it is a right He has made for Himself against them, so He has the choice to punish them, thus fulfilling His right, or to leave them, forgoing His right. As for the issue of not exiting Paradise once entered, this is supported by numerous verses and narrations. The consensus mentioned is based on what is accepted from the implications of the scripture and tradition, or reason, and is not a separate argument.

Examining Narrations

(1) In al-Durr al-manthūr, al-Suyūṭī cites al-Bukhārī, Muslim, al-Tirmidhī, al-Nasāʾī, Ibn M āja, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-M undhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Abū al-Shaykkh, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqī’s al-Asmāʾ wa al-ṣifāt, all of whom report from Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī that the Messenger of God said: ‘Indeed, God allows the wrongdoer respite, but when He seizes him, He does not let him escape.’

Then he recited: Such is the seizing of your Lord when He seizes the townships that are wrongdoing. Indeed His seizing is painful, severe (11:102).’

(2) In the same source, he cites al-Tirmidhī— who declares the tradition good (ḥasan)—and Abū Yaʿlā, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir,

Ibn Abī al-Ḥātim, Abū al-Shaykh, and Ibn Mardawayh, all of whom narrate from ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb: ‘When the verse was revealed, Some of them will be wretched and some felicitous, I said: “O Messenger of God, then why should we do anything? For something already predetermined or for something yet to be decided?” The Prophet replied, “For something already settled, ʿUmar. The pens have been lifted, and the scrolls have dried up, yet everyone will find it easy to do that for which they were created.”’ Author’s comment: This wording is narrated from the Prophet through multiple channels in Sunnī sources, as in Sahih Al-Bukhari from ʿImrān b. al-Huṣayn, who said: ‘I asked: “O Messenger of God, what do people labour for?” He said: “Everyone will find it easy to do that for which he was created.”’

(3) In the same source, it is also reported from ʿAlī , from the Prophet that he was at a funeral and took a stick and began to poke the ground. He said: ‘There is none among you who has not had his seat assigned either in Paradise or in Hellfire.’ They asked: ‘Shall we not then rely upon this and cease working?’ He replied: ‘No, carry on doing good deeds, for everyone will find it easy to do that for which he was created.’ He then recited the verse: As for him who gives and is Godwary (92:5).

Author’s comment: To clarify this, we say: It is obvious to anyone with a grain of sense that all events occurring in this world, both in their existence and their effects, are potential until they are garbed of certainty and existence. This potential means that existence and non-existence are equal in relation to them. For example, a piece of wood has the potential to become ash through burning, and a semen has the potential to become a human if it efiectively becomes part of the necessary causes for a human being, and also the potential to remain as non-human if these necessary causes cease to exist.

Once something has put on the garb of existence, such as when wood has actually become ash or semen has actually become a human, the potentiality that was attributed to it ceases, as it no longer holds the potential

to become both ash and not-ash, or human and non-human. It simply becomes a human and nothing else, or ash and nothing else, other possibilities are negated with this actuality.

In this context, it becomes clear that when we take actualized events and attribute them to their underlying causes and, by the same token, attribute these causes to the causes of causes, the world in this perspective appears as a chain of actualized events with nothing changing from

its original state of potentiality to a state of actuality. The possibilities, preparations, and alternatives all cease to exist. Conversely, when we look at things from the aspect of potentialities and possibilities that they hold latent within themselves with respect to their final forms, no physical entities escape the realm of possibility and the domain of choice.

Thus, the universe has two aspects: one of necessity and actuality, where every part of it—whether a substance or the effect of a substance—is determined and admits no ambiguity or hesitation, no changes or alterations. This is the aspect where effects rely on their originating and sufficient

causes, which are inseparable from their corollaries, and whose effects always result from them, and no trick can change them from what they are, nor any effort or motion can alter them.

The other aspect is the realm of possibility, the form of preparedness and susceptibility, where nothing is determined except after occurrence, and nothing moves from ambiguity and generality until it becomes a reality. On this plane, the laws of choice exist, and with it arises efforts and

movements, work and acquisition take place, and it is to this that education, upbringing, fear, hope, aspirations, and desires have their influence,

and where the call to action, and moral commands and prohibitions are effective, and reward and punishment become valid.

It is self-evident that these two aspects do not conflict in reality, and that one of them does not invalidate the other. Actualized phenomena have their context, and possibility and potentiality have theirs, just as the ontological ambiguity of a particular event does not prevent its realization after it has occurred, and its subsequent realization does not render

its prior ambiguity void.

The first aspect—that of ambiguity—corresponds to Divine Decree, and the actuality of events according to it does not invalidate their indeterminacy in the context of invitation, work, and acquisition. We will conclude the discussion on this when we address the topics of Divine Decree

and Destiny at the appropriate place, God willing.

Now, let’s return to our discussion of the traditions:

Reflecting on their context, it appears that what the listeners understood from the Prophet’s statement about felicity and wretchedness, paradise and hell, and the writing of the pen to that effect, that these were

predestined and unavoidable fates. Based on this, they arrived at the misconception, first, that the ways that led people to one fate or the other were

irrelevant, and that the laws of causality no longer applied, such that, if a person is destined for heaven, this will inevitably happen, regardless of whether they do good deeds or whether they commit sins.

Secondly, they believed that these ways and means are analogous to the ends and effects that fall under the Divine Decree, which is written and determined, rendering human free will meaningless and leaving no room for effort and moral responsibility.

Consider the questions posed in these traditions:

‘O Messenger of God, then why should we do anything? For something already predetermined or for something yet to be decided?’

‘O Messenger of God, what do people labour for?’

‘Shall we not then rely upon this and cease working?’

What the questioners are in fact asking is: ‘Should we not stop doing deeds and rely instead upon what God has written for us in His Book that can neither be changed nor altered?’ All of this points to their first misconception, and it is as though their own experience of free will and the

ability to act prevented them from recognizing the second one. However, these two misconceptions are intrinsically linked, and even though the second may have been deeply rooted in their hearts, they did not express it. In response to their questions, the Prophet said: ‘everyone will find it easy to do that for which he was created.’ This is an allusion to God’s description of the creation of the human being: Then He made the way easy for him (80:20). This means that those created for Heaven and those created for Hell, as stated in the verse, Certainly W e have created for hell many of the jinn and humans (7:179), each have a purpose in their creation. God has made the path to these ends easy for them and facilitated their journey to their ultimate destination.

Between a person destined for Paradise and Paradise itself, there lies a path that they must inevitably follow in order to reach it. Similarly, between a person destined for Hell and Hell itself, there lies a path. The path to Heaven is faith and piety, while the path to Hell is idolatry and sin. The person for whom Heaven has been decreed must tread the path of faith and piety. He cannot simply be granted Heaven regardless of whether he acts righteously or not, or whether his actions are good or bad. The same applies to the person for whom Hell has been decreed: his path is that of idolatry and sin, not merely an unconditional decree.

For this reason, the Prophet followed his statement, ‘everyone will find it easy to do that for which he was created’, by reciting God’s words, As for him who gives and is Godwary and confirms the best promise, We shall surely ease him into facility. But as for him who is stingy and self-complacent, and denies the best promise, We shall surely ease him into hardship (92:10). Expecting one of these two outcomes without following its respective path is like hoping to be filled without eating, or to quench one’s thirst without drinking, or to move from one place to another without actually moving. In this life, which is a realm of striving and activity, one can only achieve their goals by undertaking a journey. As God says, and that nothing belongs to man except what he strives for, and that he will soon be shown

his endeavour, then he will be rewarded for it with the fullest reward (53:41). However, even though his audience might not have explicitly voiced it, the Prophet did not fail to address the second misconception, which are expressed in the idea of ‘making easy.’ To make something easy (taysīr) means to facilitate it, and it is well known that such facilitation can only occur in matters that are not already inevitable or foreordained. If the path to Heaven were absolutely and inevitably predestined for those for whom it has been written, it would be fixed and unchangeable. There would be no meaning in facilitating or easing their journey, as should be obvious. Therefore, the Prophet’s saying, ‘everyone will find it easy to do that for which he was created’, implies that the matters which human beings incline towards, such as felicity or wretchedness, have two aspects. The first aspect is the inevitability and predetermination that cannot change its course, and the second aspect is the possibility and choice that is made easy for humans to follow through deeds and moral responsibility. The divine call to humankind is only directed to the second aspect, not the first.1 We have previously discussed predestination and free will in our commentary on the verse, and He leads no one astray thereby except the transgressors (2:26) in the first volume of this commentary.

(4) In al-Durr al-manthūr, al-Suyūṭī cites Ibn Jarīr, Abū al-Shaykh, and Ibn M ardawayh, who narrate that Qatāda recited the verse, As for the wretched … (11:106), then said: ‘Anas narrated that Messenger of God said: “A group of people will come out of the Fire.” and we do not say as the People of Harūrāʾ say.’

Author’s comment: The statement, ‘… we do not say as the People of Harūrāʾ say’, is the comment of Qatāda, not the Prophet . The People of Harūrāʾ are a sub-sect of the Khawārij, who asserted that whoever enters

(5) Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Jābir that the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, recited, “So those who were unfortunate - to His saying - except as your Lord wills,” the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, said: “If God wills to take people out of the Fire - from those who were unfortunate - and admit them into Paradise, He will do so.” (alDurr al-manthūr)

(6) In Tafsīr al-Burhān, it is narrated from al-Ḥusayn b. Saʿīd al-Ahwāzī’s Kitāb al-Zuhd, via chain of narrators from Muḥammad b. Muslim: ‘I asked Abū ʿAbd Allāh about the Hellish (jahanummiyyīn). He said: “Abū Jaʿfar used to say: ‘They will come out of it and arrive at a spring at the gates of Paradise that is called “the Spring of Life” (ʿAyn al-Ḥaywān). Its waters will sprinkle on them and they will flourish, just as plants flourish, their skin and hair will flourish.’”’

Author’s comment: It is also reported via a chain of narration from ʿUmar b. Abān from him . The meaning of jahannumiyyīn are a specific group of the inmates of Hell who are believers in monotheism (ahl

al-tawḥīd) who will be saved from Hell through intercession (shafāʿa). They are the ones called jahannumiyyīn, not everyone who dwells in Hell, as will become clear from the other traditions below.

(7) It is narrated from Abū Baṣīr, who said: ‘I heard Abū Jaʿfar say: “Indeed, there are people who will leave Hell behind. When they have become ashes, intercession will reach them.” He said, “They will be taken to a river that flows out of the land of the inhabitants of Paradise. They will bathe there, and their flesh and blood will recover. The scorching effects of Hell will disappear from them.

They will enter paradise and the inhabitants of Paradise will call them ‘the Hellish’ (jahannumiyyīn). They will unanimously call out, ‘O God, remove this name from us!’” He said, “And it will be removed from them.” Then he said, “O Abū Baṣīr, indeed the enemies of ʿAlī are the ones who will dwell in Hell forever, and intercession will not reach them.”’ (Tafsīr al-Burhān)

(8) It is narrated on the authority of ʿUmar b. Abān who said, ‘I heard a righteous servant say about the hellish: ‘”Indeed, they enter Hell because of their sins, and they will exit due to God’s pardon.”’ (ibid.)

(9) It is narrated on the authority of Ḥumrān who said, ‘I said to Abū ʿAbd Allāh : ‘They say, “Do not be amazed by a people who claim that God will bring some people out of Hell to make them dwellers of paradise along with God’s allies.” He replied, “Do they not read God’s statement, Beside these two, there will be two other gardens (55:62)? That is a garden beyond a garden, and a hell beyond a hell. They will not dwell with God’s allies.” He then said, “Between them, I swear by God, there is a station, but I cannot discuss it. Their condition is more narrow than a ring. When the Riser (Qāʾim) rises, he will start with these.”’

Author’s comment: When he says, ‘When the Riser rises…’, he means that, when he appears, he will first exact retribution upon those who mocked the people of truth.

(10) In Tafsīr al-ʿAyyāshī, it is narrated from Ḥumrān, from Abū Jaʿfar : ‘I asked him about the verse, They shall remain in it for as long as the heavens and the earth endure—except what your Lord may wish

(11:107). He said, “This is about the ones who leave Hell behind.”’ (11) It is narrated from Abū Baṣīr, from Imām al-Bāqir , concerning the verse, Some of them will be wretched and some felicitous (11:105): ‘In the description of the people of Hell, an exception was made, but there was no exception in the mention of the description of the people of Paradise: They will remain in it for as long as the heavens and the earth endure—except what your Lord may wish—an

endless bounty (11:108).’ (ibid.)

Author’s comment: Here, he points out that the exception of divine will in the case of the people of Paradise, which God followed with the statement, ‘an endless bounty’, is not an exception indicating the expulsion of some of the inhabitants of paradise from it, rather it is there to preserve God’s absolute power, unlike the exception in the case of the people of Hell, which is followed by His statement, indeed your Lord does what He desires (11:107), suggesting that this had actually taken place, as we have already discussed previously.

(12) In al-Durr al-manthūr, al-Suyūṭī narrates from Abū al-Shaykh, who narrates from al-Sudayy, about the verse, As for the wretched … (11:107): ‘Later, by the will of God, the verse was abrogated, and God revealed in Medina: Indeed those who are faithless and do wrong, Allah shall never forgive them, nor shall He guide them to any way … (4:168). Thus, any hope of release for the inhabitants of Hell was removed, meaning that they were condemned to

remain there eternally.’ Regarding the verse, As for the felicitous …, he said: ‘Later, by the will of God, the verse was abrogated, and God revealed in Medina: As for those who have faith and do righteous deeds, We shall admit them into gardens with streams running in them, to remain in them forever … (4:58), meaning that they would dwell there eternally.

Author’s comment: What this tradition says about the abrogation of these two verses implies that they indicate that they meant people would reside in Paradise and Hell only temporarily, which contradicts what we know to be the case. In such contexts, abrogation does not correspond with reason or with revelation. It also does not agree with the explicit meaning of verses concerning Paradise. Furthermore, the idea that both groups will remain in Paradise and Hell eternally is established in many M eccan chapters, including al-Anʿām and al-Aʿrāf. Therefore, there is no sense in saying that this was only revealed later, in M edina.

(13) Ibn al-M undhir reports from al-Ḥasan, who reports from ʿUmar: ‘If the inhabitants of Hell remained in it for as long as there are grains of sand, there would come a day when they would leave it.’

(al-Durr al-manthūr)

(14) Isḥāq b. Rāhawayh narrates from Abū Hurayra: ‘A day will come upon Hell when no one will remain in it.’ Then he recited the verse, As for the wretched … (11:107). (ibid.)

(15) Ibn al-Mundhir and Abū al-Shaykh narrate from Ibrāhīm, who said: ‘There is no verse in the Qur’an more hopeful for the inmates of Hell than this one: They shall remain in it for as long as the heavens and the earth endure—except what your Lord may wish

(11:107). Ibn Masʿūd once said: ‘There will come a time when its gates will be thrown open.’ (ibid.)

Author’s comment: The three above mentioned narrations are all opinions of the Companions and, as such, do not constitute a conclusive proof (ḥujja) for anyone other than themselves. If they are assumed to have interrupted chains of narration, they would be dismissed due to the fact that they contradict the Qur’an. God has said of the disbelievers: and they shall not leave the Fire (2:167).

(16) In Tafsīr al-Burhān, it is transmitted from al-Ḥusayn b. Saʿīd’s Kitāb al-Zuhd, via a chain of narrators going back to Ḥumrān: ‘I said to Abū ʿAbd Allāh : “It has reached us that there will come a time when the gates of Hell will be thrown open!” He said: “No by God, it is for eternity.” I quoted the verse, They shall remain in it for as long as the heavens and the earth endure—except what your Lord may wish. He said: ‘This is about those who will be released Hell.

Author’s comment: The narrations indicating that the disbelievers will be consigned to Hell eternally, according to the narration of the Imams of the Prophet’s Household , are extremely numerous. We have previously presented a philosophical discussion on the perpetuity of punishment and its cessation in our commentary on the verse, and they shall not leave the Fire (2:167).
